To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
perceptual load and expectations interact to determine the allocation of perceptually relevant processing resources during visual search.

top-down expectations can modulate the influence of load, and that the extent to which load modulates the brain’s response to irrelevant information is associated with individual differences in susceptibility to distraction.

the influence of load and expectation on perceptual processing are mediated by the same neural mechanisms and that the influence of expectation on perceptual distraction depends upon the extent to which perceptual demands exceed available capacity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the allocation of perceptually relevant resources is influenced by expectations.
the automaticity of attentional selection and the extent to which top-down control can be used to modulate the processing of task-relevent and irrelevant information.
the role of perceptual load and expectations in the allocation of attentional resources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perceptual load theory of attention does not account for all of the data.
our results provide evidence for the automaticity of perceptual load and the top-down biasing of attentional selection.
top-down expectations modulate perceptual load and, in doing so, modulate the allocation of attention to the processing of task-redundant and task-irrelevant stimuli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perceptual load theory of attention is partially correct.
the load theory of attention is not a complete theory because it fails to account for the influence of expectations on the allocation of attentional resources.
perceptual load is a powerful mechanism for controlling the allocation of perceptually based attentional resources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the perceptual demands imposed by the task are automatically and exhaustively consumed and that top-down expectations can modulate this automaticity.
perceptual load and expectations are not independent mechanisms that operate in isolation.
the allocation of perceptually driven resources to task-irlevant distractors can be influenced by top-down expectations.
